part4.sample: In Bristol, the idea for a neighbourhood repair café grew from conversations among residents. People wanted a practical response to reducing household waste, but they were unsure whether a small local group could make a lasting difference. Rather than launch a large programme immediately, the organisers decided to learn from the people who might use it.

paragraphs.heading: h1
paragraphs.text: The need was not identified from a national report but from repeated local conversations. Residents described how reducing household waste affected ordinary routines and pointed out that existing services did not always fit their circumstances. The organisers compared these accounts and looked for a manageable first step. Their aim was not to claim that one community project could solve a broad problem. Instead, they wanted to offer a useful local response, learn what worked and invite participants to shape the next stage. This careful beginning helped the group explain its purpose without promising more than it could deliver.

paragraphs.heading: h2
paragraphs.text: The first version of a neighbourhood repair café was deliberately small. A limited trial allowed the team to check the venue, timing and instructions before inviting a much larger audience. Participants were asked what had been clear and what had caused difficulty. Some suggestions were simple, such as changing the order of activities or sending directions earlier, while others required more planning. The organisers made a short list of changes and tested them at the next session. This approach took longer than announcing a full programme at once, but it reduced the risk of repeating avoidable mistakes and gave local people a reason to trust the project.

paragraphs.heading: h3
paragraphs.text: Making an activity available does not automatically make it accessible. The team therefore considered cost, travel, information and the needs of people who had not attended before. A session that works for someone with a flexible schedule may be difficult for a person with caring duties or a long journey. The organisers began sharing basic information in advance and asked participants to identify practical barriers privately. They also discussed whether some material could be offered online, while recognising that digital access is not equal for everyone. These adjustments were modest, but they made it easier for more residents to decide whether the activity suited them.

paragraphs.heading: h4
paragraphs.text: The project depended on more than enthusiasm. Local partners contributed time, space or specialist knowledge, and volunteers had to coordinate those contributions carefully. The group tried to make responsibilities clear so that the same people were not expected to solve every problem. When a partner could not help on a particular date, the organisers adjusted the plan instead of cancelling without explanation. This network of support gave a neighbourhood repair café access to resources it could not have paid for alone. It also created a shared sense of responsibility: residents were not simply receiving a service but helping to maintain something they valued.

paragraphs.heading: h5
paragraphs.text: Participants sometimes described benefits that were not part of the original plan. People met neighbours they had not spoken to before, exchanged advice and became more confident about contributing to other local activities. Such outcomes are difficult to measure, yet they can affect whether a project remains useful over time. The organisers did not treat these comments as proof that every participant had the same experience. Instead, they used them as prompts for further questions. The wider value of a neighbourhood repair café may therefore include both its direct response to reducing household waste and the relationships that develop while people work toward a shared goal.

paragraphs.heading: h6
paragraphs.text: The team wanted to know whether the work was making a difference, not simply whether an event had taken place. It began recording attendance, repeat visits and the questions people raised. These figures could show patterns, but they could not explain why someone stopped coming or whether the activity had helped them outside the session. For that reason, the group combined simple records with short feedback conversations. It reviewed the evidence at regular intervals and avoided presenting early results as a final verdict. This made evaluation part of the project rather than a report written only when funding or publicity was needed.

paragraphs.heading: h7
paragraphs.text: The next stage is to decide how a neighbourhood repair café can continue without losing the qualities participants appreciate. Some residents would welcome more sessions, while others worry that rapid growth could make the activity less personal or harder to organise. The team plans to compare different options, including training additional volunteers and working with another venue in Bristol. Any expansion will depend on whether suitable support is available and whether the existing group can maintain clear communication. The organisers see sustainable progress as a series of informed decisions, not a promise to grow every year. Their central measure will remain whether the project responds to real local needs.

part4.sample: In York, the idea for a riverside clean-up grew from conversations among residents. People wanted a practical response to protecting local wildlife, but they were unsure whether a small local group could make a lasting difference. Rather than launch a large programme immediately, the organisers decided to learn from the people who might use it.

paragraphs.heading: h1
paragraphs.text: The need was not identified from a national report but from repeated local conversations. Residents described how protecting local wildlife affected ordinary routines and pointed out that existing services did not always fit their circumstances. The organisers compared these accounts and looked for a manageable first step. Their aim was not to claim that one community project could solve a broad problem. Instead, they wanted to offer a useful local response, learn what worked and invite participants to shape the next stage. This careful beginning helped the group explain its purpose without promising more than it could deliver.

paragraphs.heading: h2
paragraphs.text: The first version of a riverside clean-up was deliberately small. A limited trial allowed the team to check the venue, timing and instructions before inviting a much larger audience. Participants were asked what had been clear and what had caused difficulty. Some suggestions were simple, such as changing the order of activities or sending directions earlier, while others required more planning. The organisers made a short list of changes and tested them at the next session. This approach took longer than announcing a full programme at once, but it reduced the risk of repeating avoidable mistakes and gave local people a reason to trust the project.

paragraphs.heading: h3
paragraphs.text: Making an activity available does not automatically make it accessible. The team therefore considered cost, travel, information and the needs of people who had not attended before. A session that works for someone with a flexible schedule may be difficult for a person with caring duties or a long journey. The organisers began sharing basic information in advance and asked participants to identify practical barriers privately. They also discussed whether some material could be offered online, while recognising that digital access is not equal for everyone. These adjustments were modest, but they made it easier for more residents to decide whether the activity suited them.

paragraphs.heading: h4
paragraphs.text: The project depended on more than enthusiasm. Local partners contributed time, space or specialist knowledge, and volunteers had to coordinate those contributions carefully. The group tried to make responsibilities clear so that the same people were not expected to solve every problem. When a partner could not help on a particular date, the organisers adjusted the plan instead of cancelling without explanation. This network of support gave a riverside clean-up access to resources it could not have paid for alone. It also created a shared sense of responsibility: residents were not simply receiving a service but helping to maintain something they valued.

paragraphs.heading: h5
paragraphs.text: Participants sometimes described benefits that were not part of the original plan. People met neighbours they had not spoken to before, exchanged advice and became more confident about contributing to other local activities. Such outcomes are difficult to measure, yet they can affect whether a project remains useful over time. The organisers did not treat these comments as proof that every participant had the same experience. Instead, they used them as prompts for further questions. The wider value of a riverside clean-up may therefore include both its direct response to protecting local wildlife and the relationships that develop while people work toward a shared goal.

paragraphs.heading: h6
paragraphs.text: The team wanted to know whether the work was making a difference, not simply whether an event had taken place. It began recording attendance, repeat visits and the questions people raised. These figures could show patterns, but they could not explain why someone stopped coming or whether the activity had helped them outside the session. For that reason, the group combined simple records with short feedback conversations. It reviewed the evidence at regular intervals and avoided presenting early results as a final verdict. This made evaluation part of the project rather than a report written only when funding or publicity was needed.

paragraphs.heading: h7
paragraphs.text: The next stage is to decide how a riverside clean-up can continue without losing the qualities participants appreciate. Some residents would welcome more sessions, while others worry that rapid growth could make the activity less personal or harder to organise. The team plans to compare different options, including training additional volunteers and working with another venue in York. Any expansion will depend on whether suitable support is available and whether the existing group can maintain clear communication. The organisers see sustainable progress as a series of informed decisions, not a promise to grow every year. Their central measure will remain whether the project responds to real local needs.

part4.sample: In Bath, the idea for a museum late-opening grew from conversations among residents. People wanted a practical response to making culture more accessible, but they were unsure whether a small local group could make a lasting difference. Rather than launch a large programme immediately, the organisers decided to learn from the people who might use it.

paragraphs.text: The need was not identified from a national report but from repeated local conversations. Residents described how making culture more accessible affected ordinary routines and pointed out that existing services did not always fit their circumstances. Instead, they wanted to offer a useful local response, learn what worked and invite participants to shape the next stage. paragraphs.heading: h2
paragraphs.text: The first version of a museum late-opening was deliberately small. A limited trial allowed the team to check the venue, timing and instructions before inviting a much larger audience. Participants were asked what had been clear and what had caused difficulty. Some suggestions were simple, such as changing the order of activities or sending directions earlier, while others required more planning. The organisers made a short list of changes and tested them at the next session. This approach took longer than announcing a full programme at once, but it reduced the risk of repeating avoidable mistakes and gave local people a reason to trust the project.

paragraphs.heading: h3
paragraphs.text: Making an activity available does not automatically make it accessible. The team therefore considered cost, travel, information and the needs of people who had not attended before. A session that works for someone with a flexible schedule may be difficult for a person with caring duties or a long journey. The organisers began sharing basic information in advance and asked participants to identify practical barriers privately. They also discussed whether some material could be offered online, while recognising that digital access is not equal for everyone. These adjustments were modest, but they made it easier for more residents to decide whether the activity suited them.

paragraphs.heading: h4

paragraphs.heading: h5

part4.sample: In Cardiff, the idea for a school exchange grew from conversations among residents. People wanted a practical response to building confidence across cultures, but they were unsure whether a small local group could make a lasting difference. Rather than launch a large programme immediately, the organisers decided to learn from the people who might use it.

paragraphs.heading: h1
paragraphs.text: The need was not identified from a national report but from repeated local conversations. Residents described how building confidence across cultures affected ordinary routines and pointed out that existing services did not always fit their circumstances. Instead, they wanted to offer a useful local response, learn what worked and invite participants to shape the next stage. This careful beginning helped the group explain its purpose without promising more than it could deliver.

paragraphs.heading: h2
paragraphs.text: The first version of a school exchange was deliberately small. A limited trial allowed the team to check the venue, timing and instructions before inviting a much larger audience. Participants were asked what had been clear and what had caused difficulty. Some suggestions were simple, such as changing the order of activities or sending directions earlier, while others required more planning. The organisers made a short list of changes and tested them at the next session. This approach took longer than announcing a full programme at once, but it reduced the risk of repeating avoidable mistakes and gave local people a reason to trust the project.

paragraphs.heading: h3
paragraphs.text: Making an activity available does not automatically make it accessible. The team therefore considered cost, travel, information and the needs of people who had not attended before. A session that works for someone with a flexible schedule may be difficult for a person with caring duties or a long journey. The organisers began sharing basic information in advance and asked participants to identify practical barriers privately. They also discussed whether some material could be offered online, while recognising that digital access is not equal for everyone. These adjustments were modest, but they made it easier for more residents to decide whether the activity suited them.

paragraphs.heading: h4

The group tried to make responsibilities clear so that the same people were not expected to solve every problem. When a partner could not help on a particular date, the organisers adjusted the plan instead of cancelling without explanation. This network of support gave a school exchange access to resources it could not have paid for alone. It also created a shared sense of responsibility: residents were not simply receiving a service but helping to maintain something they valued.

part4.sample: In Cambridge, the idea for a science festival grew from conversations among residents. People wanted a practical response to making research easier to understand, but they were unsure whether a small local group could make a lasting difference. Rather than launch a large programme immediately, the organisers decided to learn from the people who might use it.

paragraphs.heading: h1
paragraphs.text: The need was not identified from a national report but from repeated local conversations. Residents described how making research easier to understand affected ordinary routines and pointed out that existing services did not always fit their circumstances. The organisers compared these accounts and looked for a manageable first step. Their aim was not to claim that one community project could solve a broad problem. Instead, they wanted to offer a useful local response, learn what worked and invite participants to shape the next stage. This careful beginning helped the group explain its purpose without promising more than it could deliver.

paragraphs.heading: h2
paragraphs.text: The first version of a science festival was deliberately small. A limited trial allowed the team to check the venue, timing and instructions before inviting a much larger audience. Participants were asked what had been clear and what had caused difficulty. Some suggestions were simple, such as changing the order of activities or sending directions earlier, while others required more planning. The organisers made a short list of changes and tested them at the next session. This approach took longer than announcing a full programme at once, but it reduced the risk of repeating avoidable mistakes and gave local people a reason to trust the project.

paragraphs.heading: h3
paragraphs.text: Making an activity available does not automatically make it accessible. The team therefore considered cost, travel, information and the needs of people who had not attended before. A session that works for someone with a flexible schedule may be difficult for a person with caring duties or a long journey. The organisers began sharing basic information in advance and asked participants to identify practical barriers privately. They also discussed whether some material could be offered online, while recognising that digital access is not equal for everyone. These adjustments were modest, but they made it easier for more residents to decide whether the activity suited them.

paragraphs.heading: h4
paragraphs.text: The project depended on more than enthusiasm. Local partners contributed time, space or specialist knowledge, and volunteers had to coordinate those contributions carefully. The group tried to make responsibilities clear so that the same people were not expected to solve every problem. When a partner could not help on a particular date, the organisers adjusted the plan instead of cancelling without explanation. This network of support gave a science festival access to resources it could not have paid for alone. It also created a shared sense of responsibility: residents were not simply receiving a service but helping to maintain something they valued.

paragraphs.heading: h5
paragraphs.text: Participants sometimes described benefits that were not part of the original plan. People met neighbours they had not spoken to before, exchanged advice and became more confident about contributing to other local activities. Such outcomes are difficult to measure, yet they can affect whether a project remains useful over time. The organisers did not treat these comments as proof that every participant had the same experience. Instead, they used them as prompts for further questions. The wider value of a science festival may therefore include both its direct response to making research easier to understand and the relationships that develop while people work toward a shared goal.

paragraphs.heading: h6
paragraphs.text: The team wanted to know whether the work was making a difference, not simply whether an event had taken place. It began recording attendance, repeat visits and the questions people raised. These figures could show patterns, but they could not explain why someone stopped coming or whether the activity had helped them outside the session. For that reason, the group combined simple records with short feedback conversations. It reviewed the evidence at regular intervals and avoided presenting early results as a final verdict. This made evaluation part of the project rather than a report written only when funding or publicity was needed.

paragraphs.heading: h7
paragraphs.text: The next stage is to decide how a science festival can continue without losing the qualities participants appreciate. Some residents would welcome more sessions, while others worry that rapid growth could make the activity less personal or harder to organise. The team plans to compare different options, including training additional volunteers and working with another venue in Cambridge. Any expansion will depend on whether suitable support is available and whether the existing group can maintain clear communication. The organisers see sustainable progress as a series of informed decisions, not a promise to grow every year. Their central measure will remain whether the project responds to real local needs.

part4.sample: In Exeter, the idea for a transport survey grew from conversations among residents. People wanted a practical response to improving travel choices, but they were unsure whether a small local group could make a lasting difference. Rather than launch a large programme immediately, the organisers decided to learn from the people who might use it.

paragraphs.heading: h1
paragraphs.text: The need was not identified from a national report but from repeated local conversations. Residents described how improving travel choices affected ordinary routines and pointed out that existing services did not always fit their circumstances. The organisers compared these accounts and looked for a manageable first step. Their aim was not to claim that one community project could solve a broad problem. Instead, they wanted to offer a useful local response, learn what worked and invite participants to shape the next stage. This careful beginning helped the group explain its purpose without promising more than it could deliver.

paragraphs.heading: h2
paragraphs.text: The first version of a transport survey was deliberately small. A limited trial allowed the team to check the venue, timing and instructions before inviting a much larger audience. Participants were asked what had been clear and what had caused difficulty. Some suggestions were simple, such as changing the order of activities or sending directions earlier, while others required more planning. The organisers made a short list of changes and tested them at the next session. This approach took longer than announcing a full programme at once, but it reduced the risk of repeating avoidable mistakes and gave local people a reason to trust the project.

paragraphs.heading: h3
paragraphs.text: Making an activity available does not automatically make it accessible. The team therefore considered cost, travel, information and the needs of people who had not attended before. A session that works for someone with a flexible schedule may be difficult for a person with caring duties or a long journey. The organisers began sharing basic information in advance and asked participants to identify practical barriers privately. They also discussed whether some material could be offered online, while recognising that digital access is not equal for everyone. These adjustments were modest, but they made it easier for more residents to decide whether the activity suited them.

paragraphs.heading: h4
paragraphs.text: The project depended on more than enthusiasm. Local partners contributed time, space or specialist knowledge, and volunteers had to coordinate those contributions carefully. The group tried to make responsibilities clear so that the same people were not expected to solve every problem. When a partner could not help on a particular date, the organisers adjusted the plan instead of cancelling without explanation. This network of support gave a transport survey access to resources it could not have paid for alone. It also created a shared sense of responsibility: residents were not simply receiving a service but helping to maintain something they valued.

paragraphs.heading: h5
paragraphs.text: Participants sometimes described benefits that were not part of the original plan. People met neighbours they had not spoken to before, exchanged advice and became more confident about contributing to other local activities. Such outcomes are difficult to measure, yet they can affect whether a project remains useful over time. The organisers did not treat these comments as proof that every participant had the same experience. Instead, they used them as prompts for further questions. The wider value of a transport survey may therefore include both its direct response to improving travel choices and the relationships that develop while people work toward a shared goal.

paragraphs.heading: h6
paragraphs.text: The team wanted to know whether the work was making a difference, not simply whether an event had taken place. It began recording attendance, repeat visits and the questions people raised. These figures could show patterns, but they could not explain why someone stopped coming or whether the activity had helped them outside the session. For that reason, the group combined simple records with short feedback conversations. It reviewed the evidence at regular intervals and avoided presenting early results as a final verdict. This made evaluation part of the project rather than a report written only when funding or publicity was needed.

paragraphs.heading: h7
paragraphs.text: The next stage is to decide how a transport survey can continue without losing the qualities participants appreciate. Some residents would welcome more sessions, while others worry that rapid growth could make the activity less personal or harder to organise. The team plans to compare different options, including training additional volunteers and working with another venue in Exeter. Any expansion will depend on whether suitable support is available and whether the existing group can maintain clear communication. The organisers see sustainable progress as a series of informed decisions, not a promise to grow every year. Their central measure will remain whether the project responds to real local needs.

Mei: I agree about welcoming people, but I would keep the current schedule. More sessions are not helpful if newcomers do not know what to expect. A short introduction would make a bigger difference. Ben: That is fair; clear information should come before advertising.
audioClips.l4-1: When I first heard about a charity music event in Norwich, I thought it would be mainly about raising funds for a local shelter. I was surprised that the organisers spent time asking what participants actually needed. I found the practical demonstration most useful because I could try the process instead of only hearing an explanation. The difficult part was arranging the journey after work, so I would like clearer information about session times. I plan to return because the group was friendly and I learned something I can use outside the meeting.
audioClips.l4-2: As an organiser of a charity music event, I used to think that finding a suitable venue would be our main challenge. In fact, keeping communication clear has required more attention. Feedback showed that some residents were unsure what to bring, so we now send a short checklist in advance. We have not decided to run sessions every week; first we want to see whether volunteers can support the current programme. If the next review shows that people are benefiting and the team has enough help, we may add one extra session later in the year.

writing.context: For Parts 1–3, imagine you are signing up for activities organised by a charity music event in Norwich. The organiser is Ben. Choose either Saturday at 10 a.m. or Sunday at 2 p.m.; arrive 15 minutes before your chosen session. The two activities offered are helping with concert rehearsals and selling advance concert tickets. You may choose either activity and invent personal details.
writing.prompt: For Part 4, imagine the situation below and invent any personal or event details you need. You attended a charity concert. Write an informal email of 40–50 words to a friend describing the evening. Then write a formal email of 120–150 words to the event organiser suggesting how to increase advance ticket sales.
part1: Would you prefer the Saturday or Sunday session organised by a charity music event?
What time would you arrive before your chosen session in Norwich?
Would you choose helping with concert rehearsals or selling advance concert tickets?
Who would you invite to join you at a charity music event?
What useful item would you bring to your chosen a charity music event activity?
writing.part2: Write 20–30 words to Ben. State your chosen day, activity and one reason for choosing that activity.
part3: What interests you about a charity music event?
How could these activities benefit people in Norwich?
What would encourage you to join future activities organised by a charity music event?

speaking.instructions: Answer using your own experiences or opinions. If a task asks about an experience you have not had, you may invent a situation and say that it is imagined. For comparisons, discuss the two options named in the task.
tasks: What kind of live music do you enjoy?
Describe an event you helped organise or would like to organise.
Compare attending a small concert with attending a large festival.
Is it better for charities to hold events or ask directly for donations? Explain.
